questions.question_text:
A bag contains $4$ red, $2$ blue and $4$ green counters.
Three counters are taken out one after the other without replacement.
What is the probability of taking two red counters and one blue counter?

options.why: Counted only one order instead of all three positions for the blue counter.
Counted only two of the three possible orders.
Kept every denominator at $10$, as if the counters were replaced each time.

questions.solution_text:
$P(\text{red, red, blue}) = \frac{4}{10} \times \frac{3}{9} \times \frac{2}{8}$
$= \frac{24}{720}$
The blue counter could be taken first, second or third, so three paths each have probability $\frac{24}{720}$.
$P(\text{two reds and a blue}) = 3 \times \frac{24}{720}$
$= \frac{72}{720}$
$= \frac{1}{10}$

questions.question_text:
Standard pack of 52 cards, no jokers!
You pick two cards.
How do you work out the probability of getting two aces?

options.why: Does not reduce the number of cards after the first ace is drawn.
Leaves four aces after selecting an ace instead of three.
Adds probabilities instead of multiplying sequential dependent probabilities.

questions.solution_text: There are four aces among 52 cards. After one ace is selected, three aces remain among 51 cards. Thus $P(\text{2 aces})=\dfrac{4}{52}\times\dfrac{3}{51}$.
